look_here_first: CREW: Look for a strongly aromatic, upright mint with opposite leaves on a four-angled stem and two to six DISTINCT, spaced flower rings. Find one actual two-lipped tubular flower and the broad pink, purple, sometimes PALE bracts directly underneath its flower tier. For a stronger split from spotted horsemint (Monarda punctata), inspect the long slender bristle tips of the floral bracts and especially the narrow, bristle-like calyx teeth; do NOT identify by purple color alone.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: erect aromatic annual with four-angled mint-family stems

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: terminal inflorescence formed by separated dense flower whorls

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: upper floral bracts often conspicuously purple or purple-tinted

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: floral bracts abruptly narrowed to long bristle-like tips

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: tubular ribbed calyx with long stiff bristle-tipped teeth

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: bilabiate white to pink/lavender corollas, commonly purple-spotted or lined

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Typically a taprooted, aromatic annual of open ground; often erect 30–75 cm tall in the Williamson County botanical treatment, although height varies with site. Multiple stems or branches may support stacked flowering heads.

key_traits.label: Leaf arrangement
key_traits.text: Opposite and decussate, the opposite leaf pairs alternating their orientation up a generally four-sided mint-family stem.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Simple, generally lanceolate to oblong-lanceolate, often about 30–60 × 6–14 mm in the UT Williamson County species account, with low serrations and gland-dotted aromatic tissue; avoid using one leaf size as a strict species diagnosis.

key_traits.label: Inflorescence
key_traits.text: An interrupted flowering axis with commonly 1–5(–7) widely spaced many-flowered nodes (verticils/verticillasters) in the Williamson County material; conspicuous modified floral bracts under each dense whorl may be pink-purple, green, or pale.

key_traits.label: Floral bracts
key_traits.text: Bract = a modified leaf below the flowers, NOT a petal. Outer bracts can be colorful and end in visibly LONG narrow hairlike/bristlelike tips (aristate). Purple is common but not required: the Glass Root Garden pale-flowered observation illustrates natural color variability, not cultivar identity.

key_traits.label: Calyx
key_traits.text: Calyx = the 5-toothed, ribbed tubular cup surrounding the base of each flower. Lemon beebalm has long slender, stiff, sharply tapering calyx teeth, often with stiff hairs. Actual tooth tips require a carefully focused side/close macro; do not confuse these smaller teeth with the larger showy bracts.

lookalikes.differences: The fastest split from spotted horsemint is the long bristle-tipped bracts/calyx teeth of M. citriodora versus the shorter pointed bracts and short triangular-lanceolate calyx teeth of M. punctata.
